result:
The last streetlight on the edge of town has a habit of humming when no one is looking. Not the electrical kind of hum—more like a low, contented note, the sort a person might make after finishing a good meal and deciding, for once, not to rush the dishes. Most people walk past it without noticing. A few pause, glance up, and keep going, already rehearsing the next thing they have to say or do. But every so often someone stops long enough for the light to finish its sentence.

Tonight it was a woman in a coat two sizes too large, the sleeves swallowing her hands. She had been walking with the particular aimlessness of someone who has already completed every errand and still doesn’t want to go home. When she reached the pole she rested her shoulder against it, the way you lean on a friend who doesn’t mind silence. The hum changed pitch, almost polite, as if clearing its throat.

“Busy day?” she asked, mostly to herself.

The light brightened a fraction. In the circle it cast on the pavement, a moth traced slow figure-eights, unhurried. The woman watched it and felt, unexpectedly, that she had been given permission to do the same. She stayed until her feet grew cold and the moth finally drifted higher, toward the dark between the roofs. When she pushed off the pole the hum resumed its earlier note, steady and unsurprised, already waiting for whoever might come next.

Somewhere farther down the road a car door shut. A dog barked once and thought better of it. The streetlight kept its small, private brightness, content to illuminate nothing more dramatic than empty asphalt and the occasional drifting leaf. It had learned, over years of quiet shifts, that most of what matters arrives without announcement and leaves the same way—soft-footed, a little tired, and briefly willing to stand still.
